How to use this lab

  1. Mechanism first: use the explorers until you can predict the next step without revealing it.
  2. Then recognition: identify airway vs vessel, epithelial type, and alveolar cell from structure.
  3. Then compare: force yourself to name the one feature that actually separates look-alikes.
  4. Then practice: choose confidence before submitting. Correct-but-unsure answers stay reviewable.
  5. Finish with the exam sheet: print or scan it only after you have worked the mechanisms.
Reasoning chain to reuse:
Development/structure → tissue derivative or anatomic change → physiologic consequence → histologic/clinical finding → discriminating clue.

8. Exam sheet

Compact final review. Use it to verify what you can already explain.

Respiratory Embryology & Histology — one-page logic set

Embryology chains

Foregut endoderm → airway/alveolar epithelium + glands.
Splanchnic mesoderm → CT, smooth muscle, cartilage.

EA/TEF → poor fetal swallowing → polyhydramnios; after birth → feeding choke/cough + frothy secretions.

Oligohydramnios / CDH compression → pulmonary hypoplasia.

Diaphragm

Septum transversum descends and carries phrenic C3–C5; central tendon association.

Pleuroperitoneal membranes close posterolateral thorax–abdomen gaps.

Pleuropericardial folds → pericardial + R/L pleural cavity separation.

CDH usually left in lecture → bowel in thorax → lung compression → hypoplasia ± mediastinal shift.

Airway recognition

Friction → stratified squamous: oropharynx, laryngopharynx, true vocal fold, food-facing epiglottis.

Bronchus = cartilage. Bronchiole = no cartilage.

Terminal bronchiole = last purely conducting airway.
Respiratory bronchiole = alveoli interrupt wall.

Vessels & alveoli

Pulmonary artery = runs with airway, similar caliber.
Pulmonary vein = interlobular, solo.
Bronchial artery = small systemic nutritive vessel.

Barrier: type I → fused basal lamina → endothelium.

Type II = cuboidal + lamellar bodies + surfactant + repair.
Macrophage = debris/lysosomes, no epithelial tight-junction attachment.

High-yield pathology comparison

EntityPrimary problemFast clue
CFCFTR defect → thick mucus → poor mucociliary clearanceCilia can work; cargo is too thick
Prematurity RDSInadequate surfactant → high surface tension/collapsePrematurity / functional immaturity
SP-B deficiencyGenetic surfactant dysfunctionPersistent severe problem, not simple maturation lag
A1AT deficiencyUnopposed protease injury → septal destructionEmphysema younger than expected
EmphysemaAlveolar walls destroyedEnlarged spaces, missing septa
PneumoniaAlveoli filled with inflammatory exudate/WBCsSpaces filled, walls not primarily destroyed

Common traps

1) Early shorthand “respiratory = alveoli” is less precise than the later transition: respiratory zone starts at respiratory bronchioles. 2) Do not distinguish pulmonary artery vs vein by wall thickness alone. 3) Type II and macrophages can both show lamellar-looking material—use tight-junction attachment. 4) Trachea vs bronchus may be ambiguous on oblique section; bronchus vs bronchiole is much safer. 5) Rare TEF configurations and detailed laryngeal labels were explicitly de-emphasized.

9. Sources & clarifications

What was used, what was adapted, and where the lecture needed a precision note.

Lecture materials used

Slide deck: 9-9-2026_Lowrie_Embryology_and_Histology_of_the_Respiratory_System_POST.V1 (1).pptx

Transcript: Embryology and Histo-transcript.txt

Objectives: 9-9-2026_Lowrie_Embryology_Histology_Respiratory_System_Objectives.V1 (1).docx

No separate professor quiz, case packet, or answer key was attached. Questions labeled “Adapted professor prompt” were built from explicit questions/reasoning prompts in the transcript; all other questions are original.

Adaptation rules used

Lecture wording and professor emphasis were kept central. Low-priority material the professor explicitly de-emphasized was not inflated into major test content.

Actual lecture slides were rendered and embedded for the figure lab. Supplemental physiology is clearly labeled; no invented numerical clinical data are presented.

Practice answer positions are shuffled deterministically in the browser, while correctness is tracked by option identity so the key does not break.

Transcript-quality limitation: the sentence describing Kulchitsky-cell lineage is garbled in the transcript. Because the slide and learning objectives do not require a lineage claim, this guide does not test that phrase. The lecture-supported points retained are neuroendocrine identity and association with small-cell carcinoma.
